title: String
short: Text as an array of characters you can read but not change.
what: A string is a row of characters, so it works like an array: s[0] is the first letter and len(s) is its length. One big difference: a Python string can never change. Every edit builds a new string.
analogy: A word printed on a receipt. You can read any letter, but to fix a typo you print a new receipt.

frames.label: s
frames.say: s = "racecar" is 7 characters in a row. s[0] is 'r', s[6] is 'r', and len(s) is 7.

frames.label: s
frames.say: Is it a palindrome, the same both ways? Put L at the start and R at the end, and compare s[0] with s[6].

frames.label: s
frames.say: Both are 'r', a match. Step both pointers inward. s[1] and s[5] are both 'a'.

frames.label: s
frames.say: Match again. Step in once more: s[2] and s[4] are both 'c'.

frames.label: s
frames.say: L and R meet at 'e' in the middle. Every pair matched, so "racecar" is a palindrome. 3 checks for 7 letters.

frames.label: s
frames.say: Try s[0] = 'R'. Python raises TypeError: strings cannot change in place.

frames.label: new string
frames.say: Instead build a new string: 'R' + s[1:] glues 'R' onto a copy of the rest. s itself is untouched.

when: Count the letters in a word
python:
s = "racecar"
print(len(s), s[0], s[-1])
print(s == s[::-1])
print("R" + s[1:])
words = ["data", "is", "fun"]
print(" ".join(words))
print("a,b,c".split(","))
print(sorted("cab"), ord("a"), chr(98))
output:
7 r r
True
Racecar
data is fun
['a', 'b', 'c']
['a', 'b', 'c'] 97 b
watch: s[i] = 'x' fails. Turn it into a list, change the list, then "".join it back.
Building a string with += in a loop can copy it every time. Collect pieces in a list and join once.
s[::-1] and s[1:] make new copies, which costs O(n) time and memory.
interview: LC 3 Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
